reason: B gives the reason behind each choice (Postgres over Redis or sticky sessions, the database clock as the one source of time, an advisory lock so concurrent failures across instances are not miscounted), defines the terms a newcomer would need, and names its remaining gaps honestly; A's overview and failure table are cleaner, but it leaves concurrency out and explains less of why the design works.

author: haiku
reason: B opens with what the app is today (server-rendered, two instances, no sign-in), gives a one-paragraph walkthrough of the whole flow, and backs it with a precise diagram, per-step notes on which tables each step touches, and a single failure table, so the system is quicker to grasp than in A, which spends space defining things a technical engineer already knows (cookies, rows, primary keys), even though A covers the lockout race more thoroughly.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A opens with a short overview, defines its terms, and then follows the request flow in order, with a diagram and numbered steps that match each other, so a newcomer can follow the system from start to finish; Document B has more exact detail (SQL, hashed IDs, cookie attributes), but it puts the rules ahead of the flow, leaves the diagram for the end, and spreads the failure rules across sections.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to learn the system from: it opens with the setup (a server-rendered app on two instances with no sticky sessions, and what is out of scope), defines its terms, and then walks through each request step by step, ending with failure cases and the choices that weren't in the brief, while A is more precise but grouped by design decision with the flow diagram at the end.

author: haiku
reason: B is the better handover for a newcomer: it explains how things work today, defines the deployment terms it relies on (pod, image, rolling deploy, readiness probe), and states what follows from the design, such as lost capacity during a store outage; it also adds tests, per-pod checks and the provider dual-key pre-check, while A is tighter but takes more of this for granted.

author: haiku
reason: A suits a reader who doesn't know the stack because it defines the infrastructure terms (pod, readiness probe, rolling deploy, image), explains the current and target behaviour step by step, and gives every rollout step the same trigger/change/state/failure layout; it also flags the unconfirmed two-keys-at-once assumption that B's rotation step skips, even though B's failure table and candid open questions are good.

author: sonnet
reason: A defines its terms first, explains how the app reads keys at runtime before it describes the rollout, and ends with a single failure table, so an outsider can build a picture of the system quickly. B is operationally thorough but puts the runtime mechanism last and has the rollout steps point forward to it (R1, R4), and its repeated per-step template makes it harder to read.

author: sonnet
reason: B reads in a better order for someone new to the system: a glossary first, then the rules that always hold, then how the app reads keys at runtime, then the rollout, a failure table and clearly marked open questions; A makes the reader jump ahead to Part 2 (R1–R5) to follow its rollout steps.

author: haiku
reason: B splits the system into one diagram per flow, names the endpoints and table columns, and explains why each check exists (the fast token check first, the conditional update as the real race guard), so it is easier to learn from than A, which tells the same mechanism two or three times and whose main extra is a smaller point about where the queue runs.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the system more clearly, with one diagram per flow that shows which component does each step, a separate revoked_at column instead of B's reuse of "used time" for revoked links, and less repetition, while still covering the same failure cases; B's extra open questions are useful but its combined diagram, step list, rules and table repeat each other.

author: sonnet
reason: B is more concrete about how the system works: it gives the table schema, the endpoints, the conditional UPDATE that enforces single use, and a row lock that stops parallel requests from beating the rate limit (A misses that race), and it says which check actually enforces the rule and which only produce friendly errors, though A's opening summary and glossary are easier for a newcomer to get into.

author: sonnet
reason: B is better for someone new to the project: it opens with the existing system and the feature's purpose, defines its terms (token, dead token, session, email queue), and ends with a failure table and open questions, while A is precise but terse and expects the reader to work out the context from its diagram and SQL.

author: haiku
reason: I'd rather be handed A: it starts with how password login works today, then gives a three-part overview and numbered steps that each say what triggers them, so a newcomer can follow the whole system in order, while B relies on a diagram plus scattered rules.

author: haiku
reason: B is the one I would rather be handed: it opens with how password login works today and why accounts are matched by sub, walks through each step with what starts it, and covers cases that A leaves out (Redis being unavailable, an email that matches an account with no password, and the cookie and CSRF details), so a newcomer can follow both the design and its reasons.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to get into: it explains the existing system, defines its terms, and lists every new endpoint and table before the flow. Its state tables (split into permanent and temporary) and its failure and message tables cover every piece, including the cookies and database errors, while A sends the reader through long numbered prose and leaves the browser-binding gap as an open question.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with a table of every new endpoint, table and cookie, then walks through every branch and failure with exact user messages and state lifetimes, and it closes the login-CSRF gap that B leaves as an open question, so a newcomer gets a complete and consistent picture of how the system works.

author: haiku
reason: B reads more easily and has two details A lacks: it removes duplicate rows from staging and it defines the checksum. I would still rather be handed A, because its opening summary, the trigger and failure behaviour given for each step, the failures table, and its handling of hangs, catching up after missed nights and re-runs give a newcomer a fuller and more reliable picture of how the system actually behaves.

author: haiku
reason: B opens with a one-paragraph summary of the whole mechanism, then adds a failure table and edge cases that A leaves out: hung attempts, catching up after a missed night, reconciliation overlapping the nightly run, and clock skew. That gives a newcomer a fuller picture of how the system actually behaves, even though A is tighter and explains the lookback more clearly.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to skim and has the clearer diagram, but A answers more of a newcomer's questions: who owns retries and records crashes or timeouts, how reconciliation avoids sharing staging with a nightly attempt, the full table of failure outcomes, how to roll it out, and what is still undecided.

author: sonnet
reason: B is longer, but it opens with a plain summary, defines every term an outsider would trip on (replica, scheduler, run, kind), names which component owns retries and how it detects failures, and explains crash and timeout handling, the first run, catch-up after a failed night, rollout and open questions, so it gives a fuller picture of how the system really behaves than A's tighter but thinner account.

author: haiku
reason: A explains why each step exists, how each component behaves when it fails, and where the design has gaps, and its terms and failure table are well organised; B is shorter and has a cleaner flow and a better replay lookback, but it skips failure behaviour, never says where the IP and user-agent data for enrichment come from, and states guarantees such as what a "closed day" means without saying how they are enforced.

author: haiku
reason: A is shorter and its flow is easier to follow, but B gives a newcomer a fuller picture of how the system actually works: why it is shaped this way, how each reader tracks its log position, where the request metadata goes, what happens in each failure, and which gaps are still open.

author: sonnet
reason: A defines every term an outsider needs, including acknowledged, raw log partition and closed day, and explains why each mechanism exists, such as why dedup is needed and why the TTL is 8 days; its failure table and full list of open questions show how the system behaves when parts break, which B leaves scattered or unstated.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains more of how the system actually behaves: why all copies of an event reach the same worker (raw log partitioned by event_id), how clock skew and crashes affect dedup, what happens at each failure point (the failure table), and what is still undecided, while A is cleaner but leaves those parts implicit.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a quick "how the pieces fit" overview, explains concepts an outsider may not know (keyset paging, ETag, unique index), and states for each step what starts it, where its state lives and how it fails, which makes the system easier to understand than A's tighter version, even though B puts the table migration in with the runtime steps.

author: haiku
reason: A's per-step "starts when / where state lives / if it fails" structure and its exact definitions (keyset paging, at-least-once retries, the email/upload state on the record) explain the system more completely and consistently, while B is tighter but contradicts itself by saying the POST does no export work right before streaming the small CSV inside it.

author: sonnet
reason: B is longer, but each step says what triggers it, what state it changes and what happens when it fails, and it covers the cases A leaves open or gets wrong: A loses the success email when a retry follows a failed send, and it never handles a crash between the insert and the enqueue, which B flags as an open point.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with a clear background on the existing system, then walks through every step in the same pattern: what triggers it, what state it keeps, and what happens when it fails. Its failure handling is also more complete and correct: if the email fails after the file is built, the retry re-sends only the email, whereas B's retry stops at done and the email is never sent.

author: haiku
reason: B opens with a plain overview of what exists today and why the check is being added, then walks through each step and adds a failure table and a list of open questions, so a newcomer sees the whole mechanism and its gaps (per-instance cache drift, the undefined Enterprise and Key Service cases, counts left behind on timeout); A is shorter and easier to read but leaves those edges unstated.
